summary.text:
The clearest stated borrowing rule we have come across. Middlesbrough's strategy takes long-term PWLB 'when interest rates reached a trigger rate of below 4.75%', with short-term borrowing capped at 20% of gross debt if that condition is not met. At 31 March 2026 the certainty curve started at 5.04% for one year, so the trigger sat below every point on it.

They nonetheless drew £45m of long-term PWLB during the year plus £5m short-term, against £7.5m of maturities and £15.353m of annuity repayments — a net £27.147m increase taking external debt to £280.589m at 4.02%. Under-borrowing is £27.221m or 8.8%, which they note is below the 10-15% most authorities run, and Table 4 plans to take it to 2.3% next year — roughly £45m more external borrowing in 2026/27.

Four of their identities reconcile exactly. The awkward corner is £13.000m of bank debt at 6.83% from the early 2000s which, under its own terms, cannot be refinanced in the short term. One officer address is published.

officer.subject: Your 4.75% trigger against today's curve
officer.body:
Hi Justin,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts ahead of Audit Committee on 3 September. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

Your outturn report has something we almost never see: an explicit, numeric borrowing rule. Paragraph 3.31 says long-term PWLB is taken "when interest rates reached a trigger rate of below 4.75%", with short-term borrowing capped at 20% of gross debt if the condition isn't met. Publishing the trigger rather than describing the intention makes the whole strategy testable, which is a good thing to be able to do in front of a committee.

Which is why the current curve is worth putting next to it. At 31 March the PWLB certainty curve started at 5.04% for one year and ran to 5.72% at ten, so the trigger already sat below every point on it. Today it's 4.95% at one year, 5.34% at five and 5.83% at ten — the very short end has dipped slightly, the rest hasn't. Bank Rate is 3.75% and the one-year OIS is about 4.11%, so the market is currently pricing up rather than down.

That matters because Table 4 plans to take under-borrowing from 8.8% to 2.3% next year, which is roughly £45m of further external borrowing in 2026/27. If the trigger holds as written, the decision becomes when rather than whether — and where on the curve the trigger first becomes reachable is a question our rates page answers in ten seconds, both fixings, whole curve: pwlbtoday.org/dashboard.

Four of your identities reconcile exactly, incidentally, which is worth saying. Opening CFR plus borrowing less MRP gives £307.810m; CFR less under-borrowing gives £280.589m; the three debt lines sum to it; and the new borrowing less maturities and annuity repayments gives the £27.147m increase. That's a clean set of books.

The awkward corner is the £13.000m of bank debt at 6.83% from the early 2000s which, under its own terms, can't be refinanced short term. We price every council's PWLB book daily against the DMO's repayment curve at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis, so the premium or discount on the rest is a lookup — never a quote, the DMO's is binding, but an answer you can get any morning. And the monthly sector breakdown at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity shows what the market is actually doing: July was £368m across 33 loans from 19 borrowers, average 5.02%.

On training, three fit Middlesbrough: Strategic PWLB borrowing, for the 2026/27 decision; Interest rate risk; and our liability benchmark pathway, which is interactive and built on live data — worth a look given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Codes, and useful context for the affordability threshold question your paragraph 3.28 raises. For members, Audit Committee Chair (Treasury) is written for exactly this committee. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
